> **Status note (remove before publishing).** This is a draft tutorial, written to accompany the paper *Local Feature Relevance and Cluster Order Selection in Model-Based Clustering for Mixed Data via Variational Inference*. It is not part of the manuscript itself and is held back from publication until the paper is posted to arXiv.

## What This Tutorial Covers

The Iris tutorial showed the package on a small, well-understood continuous dataset.
This one stress-tests a different axis: **how does `NaiveMFLFRMixDClust` perform when most
features are categorical, some with many levels, and none carry any usable semantic
meaning?** The UCI [Statlog Australian Credit Approval](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/143/statlog+australian+credit+approval)
dataset is built for exactly this kind of test - and unlike Iris, it comes with a
genuine binary outcome label (loan approved/rejected), so we can compute an Adjusted
Rand Index (ARI) against external ground truth.

## The Dataset

This dataset concerns credit card applications. Per the UCI documentation:
*"All attribute names and values have been changed to meaningless symbols to protect
confidentiality of the data."* It has $n=690$ applications, 6 continuous and 8
categorical attributes (`A1`-`A14`), and a binary class label (1 = approved, 0 =
rejected; 307 approved, 383 rejected). Missing values (5% of cases) were imputed in
the standard release used here (mode for categorical, mean for continuous).

| Attribute | Type | Levels / notes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `A1` | categorical | 2 levels |
| `A2` | continuous | |
| `A3` | continuous | |
| `A4` | categorical | 3 levels |
| `A5` | categorical | 14 levels |
| `A6` | categorical | 8 levels |
| `A7` | continuous | |
| `A8` | categorical | 2 levels |
| `A9` | categorical | 2 levels |
| `A10` | continuous | integer-valued, zero-inflated (median 0, max 67) |
| `A11` | categorical | 2 levels |
| `A12` | categorical | 3 levels |
| `A13` | continuous | |
| `A14` | continuous | extreme right skew - `log1p`-transformed before standardization |
| `class` | label (not a feature) | 1 = approved, 0 = rejected |

`A5` (14 levels) and `A6` (8 levels) make this a useful test of the Multinomial margin
at higher cardinality than UCI Heart Disease or Iris.

## Setup

```{julia}
using NaiveMFLFRMixDClust
using CSV, DataFrames, Statistics, Random, Printf
```

## Loading and Preparing the Data

```{julia}
df = CSV.read(joinpath(@__DIR__, "../data/australian_credit.csv"), DataFrame)
println("n = $(nrow(df)),  columns = $(names(df))")
first(df, 3)
```

```{julia}
feature_names = ["A2","A3","A7","A10","A13","A14","A1","A4","A5","A6","A8","A9","A11","A12"]

function onehot(val, levels)
    idx = findfirst(==(val), levels)
    isnothing(idx) && error("Value $val not in $levels")
    v = zeros(Int, length(levels)); v[idx] = 1; v
end

dataset = Vector{Any}(undef, 14)
dataset[1]  = Float64.(df.A2)
dataset[2]  = Float64.(df.A3)
dataset[3]  = Float64.(df.A7)
dataset[4]  = Float64.(df.A10)
dataset[5]  = Float64.(df.A13)
dataset[6]  = log1p.(Float64.(df.A14))   # log1p for extreme right skew
dataset[7]  = [onehot(x, [0, 1])              for x in df.A1]
dataset[8]  = [onehot(x, [1, 2, 3])           for x in df.A4]
dataset[9]  = [onehot(x, collect(1:14))       for x in df.A5]
dataset[10] = [onehot(x, [1,2,3,4,5,7,8,9])  for x in df.A6]
dataset[11] = [onehot(x, [0, 1])              for x in df.A8]
dataset[12] = [onehot(x, [0, 1])              for x in df.A9]
dataset[13] = [onehot(x, [0, 1])              for x in df.A11]
dataset[14] = [onehot(x, [1, 2, 3])           for x in df.A12]

# Standardize continuous features
for j in 1:6
    m = mean(dataset[j]); s = std(dataset[j])
    dataset[j] = (dataset[j] .- m) ./ s
end

labels_true = Vector{Int}(df.class)
println("Class distribution: $(count(==(1), labels_true)) approved, $(count(==(0), labels_true)) rejected")
```

## Fitting the Model

We fit both model settings with $K_{\text{fit}}=10$, $u^{(0)}=0.01$.

### SFRM - Shared Feature Relevance Model

```{julia}
Random.seed!(42)
res_sfrm = mixClust(dataset, 10;
                    model_setting = SFRM(),
                    u0       = 0.01,
                    max_iter = 3000,
                    tol      = 1e-5,
                    compact  = true)

K_sfrm = size(res_sfrm.w, 2)
@printf("SFRM → K̂ = %d clusters (converged in %d / 3000 iterations)\n",
        K_sfrm, length(res_sfrm.elbo_history))
println("Cluster sizes: ", [count(==(k), res_sfrm.labels) for k in 1:K_sfrm])
```

### LFRM - Local Feature Relevance Model

```{julia}
Random.seed!(42)
res_lfrm = mixClust(dataset, 10;
                    model_setting = LFRM(),
                    u0       = 0.01,
                    max_iter = 3000,
                    tol      = 1e-5,
                    compact  = true)

K_lfrm = size(res_lfrm.w, 2)
@printf("LFRM → K̂ = %d clusters (converged in %d / 3000 iterations)\n",
        K_lfrm, length(res_lfrm.elbo_history))
println("Cluster sizes: ", [count(==(k), res_lfrm.labels) for k in 1:K_lfrm])
```

## External Validation: A Cautionary Result {#sec-ari}

Unlike Iris, this dataset has a real binary outcome - the credit approval decision
- so we can compute ARI against it. The result is worth reporting honestly.

```{julia}
function compute_ari(labels_true, labels_pred)
    n = length(labels_true)
    classes  = unique(labels_true)
    clusters = unique(labels_pred)
    C, K = length(classes), length(clusters)
    cont = zeros(Int, C, K)
    for i in 1:n
        ci = findfirst(==(labels_true[i]),  classes)
        ki = findfirst(==(labels_pred[i]), clusters)
        cont[ci, ki] += 1
    end
    s_ij = sum(x -> x*(x-1)/2, cont)
    s_i  = sum(x -> x*(x-1)/2, sum(cont, dims=2))
    s_j  = sum(x -> x*(x-1)/2, sum(cont, dims=1))
    exp  = (s_i * s_j) / (n*(n-1)/2)
    mx   = 0.5*(s_i + s_j)
    mx == exp && return 1.0
    return (s_ij - exp) / (mx - exp)
end

ari_sfrm = compute_ari(labels_true, res_sfrm.labels)
ari_lfrm = compute_ari(labels_true, res_lfrm.labels)

conf_sfrm = mean(maximum(res_sfrm.w[i, :]) for i in 1:nrow(df))
conf_lfrm = mean(maximum(res_lfrm.w[i, :]) for i in 1:nrow(df))

println("Summary")
println("─────────────────────────────────────────────")
@printf("  %-6s  K̂ = %d   ARI = %.3f   confidence = %.3f\n",
        "SFRM", K_sfrm, ari_sfrm, conf_sfrm)
@printf("  %-6s  K̂ = %d   ARI = %.3f   confidence = %.3f\n",
        "LFRM", K_lfrm, ari_lfrm, conf_lfrm)
```

Both SFRM and LFRM score *below* plain K-means (K=2 fixed, ARI ≈ 0.314) - the
opposite of the UCI Heart Disease result. The reason: K-means forced to $K=2$ is
by construction aligned with a binary label. Our model finds finer subpopulation
structure ($\widehat{K}=5$-$6$) than the approve/reject boundary distinguishes,
which mechanically incurs ARI penalties even when the finer clusters are internally
coherent - as the assignment-confidence numbers above confirm.

::: {.callout-note}
**ARI against a binary label is not a fair test of automatic order selection.**
A finer, more confident partition that subdivides each side of the true binary
decision will always be penalized by ARI against that label, even if it is a better
description of the actual feature-space structure. Whether to trust the automatically
selected $\widehat{K}$ or to also check against a label-matched $K$ depends on
whether the label itself reflects the population's true subgroup structure.
:::

## Does the Cluster Structure Help Downstream Prediction? {#sec-predictive}

We tested two ways to exploit the discovered cluster structure for predicting loan
approval, using 10-fold stratified cross-validation (Python scripts
`experiments/scripts/australian_predictive_cv.py` and `australian_moe_cv.py`):

1. **Feature augmentation** - soft cluster-membership weights added as extra predictors.
2. **Mixture of experts** - a separate classifier per cluster, weighted by membership.

| Feature set | Classifier | Accuracy | AUC |
| :--- | :--- | :---: | :---: |
| Baseline (raw features) | LogisticRegression | 0.859 ± 0.049 | 0.928 ± 0.040 |
| Baseline (raw features) | RandomForest | 0.870 ± 0.040 | 0.934 ± 0.040 |
| + SFRM cluster membership | LogisticRegression | 0.861 ± 0.045 | 0.930 ± 0.037 |
| + SFRM cluster membership | RandomForest | 0.870 ± 0.055 | 0.930 ± 0.042 |
| + LFRM cluster membership | LogisticRegression | 0.858 ± 0.046 | 0.928 ± 0.039 |
| + LFRM cluster membership | RandomForest | 0.862 ± 0.048 | 0.931 ± 0.042 |
| Mixture of experts, SFRM | per-cluster LogisticRegression | 0.852 ± 0.053 | 0.910 ± 0.041 |
| Mixture of experts, LFRM | per-cluster LogisticRegression | 0.852 ± 0.061 | 0.907 ± 0.047 |

Neither approach helps. Feature augmentation is a wash; the mixture of experts is
slightly *worse* (splitting $n=690$ into 5-6 per-cluster regressions leaves too few
observations per expert). This is a useful negative result: discovering finer cluster
structure does not automatically translate into better downstream prediction at this
sample size.

## Takeaways

- `NaiveMFLFRMixDClust` handles high-cardinality categorical features (up to 14 levels) and
  a fully anonymized feature set without numerical difficulty.
- LFRM surfaces features whose relevance is locally concentrated rather than uniform -
  consistent with the pattern found on UCI Heart Disease in the main manuscript.
- **ARI against an external label is not always going to favor automatic order
  selection over a fixed-$K$ baseline** - and that is not necessarily a failure of
  the method.
- **Discovering finer cluster structure does not automatically translate into better
  downstream prediction** - a useful negative result for anyone tempted to assume
  "more structure found" implies "more useful for prediction."
